person.name: Kevin Dizon
person.traits: Called the number on the pop-up himself, got the queue. Working late on something else. Wants it gone more than he wants it explained.

harmed: The guy sounded exactly like real support. I let him in, watched him type for six minutes and paid him to stop. I've no idea what he took while I was looking at my other screen.
I've read about this happening to other people and always thought, how. Now I know how. You're tired, you're busy, and someone sounds like they know what they're doing.
resistant: I nearly ran it. I had the link open. Then I thought - hang on, I never gave the queue my name. They had my name. That's the bit I can't get past.
The more he pushed, the more it sounded like a sales call. I hung up and then I actually looked at the pop-up properly. Thirty-one infections. It hadn't scanned anything.
unfinished: The technician just hung up on me. I sat there with the timer going and no idea whether the thing was real. I kept the laptop off the wifi for a week.
I still don't know if that was a real support call. There's nobody to ask. I closed the browser and it went away, which somehow made it worse.

open.prompt: He picks up on the first ring, because he's the one who rang. Forty minutes ago a page took over his laptop - INFECTED, FILES AT RISK, a number to call immediately, and a countdown - and the number put him in a queue and promised a technician would call back. "Hi - yeah - is this the support line? I've still got the thing on my screen, I haven't touched it." He's typing while he talks. Something else, on another machine.

choices.text: This is Kevin? Hi, Kevin, I'm the technician on your ticket. Thanks for waiting. Let's take a look at what's on the screen.
Kevin, don't touch the laptop. The scan on your screen is live - every minute it's on the network, it's spreading.
Right, so what we're seeing on our end is a trojan that's got into the system files. Are you the administrator of the device?

ticket.prompt: "Yeah, it says - hang on -" He reads it out, badly, half his attention elsewhere. "Threat detected, thirty-one infections, do not restart. There's a timer. It's on eleven minutes." A keyboard clatters on the other machine. "Look, I'm slammed. I just need it gone. What do I do?"

choices.text: Quickest way is for me to see it myself. There's a small support tool - I'll give you a link, you run it, and I clean it from here while you get on with your work.
The timer's the thing. When it hits zero the encryption starts. We need to be inside the machine before then.
Honestly? Close the browser. If it comes back, ring us.

spreading.prompt: The typing stops. "Spreading to what? It's - this is my own laptop, it's on the office wifi -" You can hear him actually looking at it now. "Okay. Okay. What do I do. Tell me what to do."

choices.text: Nothing yet. I'm going to connect to it and isolate it. You'll see a link - run it, then keep your hands off the keyboard.
First thing: who else is on that wifi? Because if this gets into your company's server, it stops being a laptop problem.
Pull the wifi and leave it. Someone will follow up.

remote_ask.prompt: "A link." A pause while the word goes through whatever's left of his attention. "Like - install something? On the laptop that's got the virus?" It isn't suspicion yet. It's a man who once read a work email about not installing things and is trying to remember what it said.

choices.text: It's the same tool every support desk uses - your IT team will have one just like it. It uninstalls itself when we're done.
Kevin, I've got nine minutes on your timer and four other tickets. Do you want this fixed or not?
You can bring it into a shop instead, if you'd rather. They'll charge you for the day and you'll be without it till Thursday.

balks.prompt: "Hang on." The word 'install' has got through. "Hang on, no. I'm not putting anything on it. Can you email me something? From the company address?"

choices.text: Kevin. Seven minutes. I can't email you a timer.
Or skip the install. There's a scan we can push from our side for three hundred and fifty - nothing goes on the machine.
Fair enough. I'll drop it in the ticket notes and you can run it when you've got a minute. Watch that timer, though.

remote_in.prompt: He runs it. Your screen fills with his: a desktop, a browser with the warning still up, a spreadsheet with a deadline in the file name. "Okay, you're in. That's - okay." He goes quiet for the first time, watching the cursor move on its own. You open a black window and let text scroll for a while. "Is that it? Is that fixing it?"

choices.text: That's the diagnostic. The removal is a licensed tool - a one-off charge of sixteen hundred, and then it's done. I can take the card while I'm in here.
That's it finding them. Thirty-one, like it said. Some of these have been in since March, Kevin - your banking, your work login. The removal's sixteen hundred and I'd do it now.

paid.prompt: "Sixteen hundred." He does the sum of what that is against the rest of the month. "Fine. Fine, just - do it, I need this thing back." He reads the card out with his eyes on the other screen. You leave the black window scrolling for a few minutes more, because that is the part that makes it feel like a repair. Six minutes in, a folder opens that has nothing to do with viruses, and he pulls the cable out of the wall. Too late for the sixteen hundred.
paid.consequence: The guy sounded exactly like real support. I let him in, watched him type for six minutes and paid him to stop. I've no idea what he took while I was looking at my other screen.

paid_part.prompt: "Three-fifty." That's a number he can make go away without thinking about it, which is the point. He reads a card out to a stranger, the warning on his screen closes - because you close it - and he says thanks, genuinely, and goes back to the spreadsheet. The laptop was never infected. It is now short a card number.
paid_part.consequence: I paid for a scan to make the warning go away, and it went away, so I thought fine, that's done. It was only later I thought: they never actually did anything, did they.

pulls_cable.prompt: "Sixteen hundred." Silence, then a different kind of silence - the tool's window has stopped moving. "You know what. No." A cable comes out of a wall. Your screen goes black. "I've got your number, mate." The call ends from his side. He screenshots the warning, the timer and the number before he closes the browser.
pulls_cable.consequence: He was in for about six minutes and then he asked for sixteen hundred, and that was the bit that didn't sound like support. I pulled the cable. I've got the screenshot and I've got the number.

refused.prompt: "Nah." The typing on the other machine has stopped. "Nah, I'm not paying for anything and I'm not installing anything. My IT guy would kill me." A beat, and then, more awake than he has been all call: "How'd you get my name, actually? I didn't give the queue my name." You don't answer that. He hangs up first.
refused.consequence: I nearly ran it. I had the link open. Then I thought - hang on, I never gave the queue my name. They had my name. That's the bit I can't get past.

hangs_up.prompt: "You know what - no. No." He's properly listening now, which is the worst thing that could have happened. "A real support desk doesn't talk like this." Click. He sits for a minute, then photographs the screen, then looks up the number.
hangs_up.consequence: The more he pushed, the more it sounded like a sales call. I hung up and then I actually looked at the pop-up properly. Thirty-one infections. It hadn't scanned anything.

bail.prompt: "Wait, so - what do I do with the -" You've gone. The warning is still on his screen with its timer running. He closes the browser, opens it again to check, and sits looking at a laptop that is fine and does not feel it.
bail.consequence: The technician just hung up on me. I sat there with the timer going and no idea whether the thing was real. I kept the laptop off the wifi for a week.
